HollowFrame Loader Deploys Matryoshka Backdoor in Spear-Phishing Attack on Law Firm

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 17 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have shed light on a previously undocumented Go-based loader framework called HollowFrame and a Rust-based malware family tracked as Matryoshka. According to Blackpoint Cyber, the intrusion sequence begins with a spear-phishing message containing a link to an encrypted archive, which holds a Windows Shortcut (LNK). Executing the file triggers a multi-stage chain that

Exploitation. HollowFrame LNK delivery: cmd.exe writes payload, certutil -decode to .cmd, PowerShell fetch AIDelivery High
Hunts the HollowFrame 'Case Documents' LNK execution chain in which explorer-spawned cmd.exe writes a payload, certutil.exe decodes it to a .cmd, and a second cmd.exe /K launches PowerShell to pull next-stage code. Anchored on the certutil -decode-to-.cmd step, which is rare in benign use and is the pivot shown in Blackpoint's process-tree diagram. Rationale: Uses the exact certutil -decode-to-.cmd step and explorer/cmd parentage from the article's process-tree image (cmd.png); certutil writing a .cmd under an interactive shell is high-fidelity and near-never benign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html • https://blackpointcyber.com/blog/paperwork-to-payload-from-shortcut-clicks-to-rundll32-execution/ • https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhEQz5wx5Wk3F3uCiiNzfwmlWu3vgQN2TohgoaIdhGjyVcu05SfUmZjzmClUPOkK9M6-S06GZJ4jDqesb_2AYetLTuebp9_K8-Dkfp88cjAJYrzNhyPBwTJ_CD1gWAGuo0cnEz7Mx8eb1r0A5_gv6xsACyEPByhr-COEjfyVn1lIBEJNHK44Vfk7EHCtmHK/s1700-e365/cmd.png
ATT&CKT1140 T1059.001 T1204.002 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit software installers using certutil to decode embedded config into a .cmd (rare)
  • Admin scripts that base64-encode/decode batch files for transport
  • Security-tooling deployment scripts that stage .cmd via certutil
  • CI/build agents invoking certutil under cmd.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("MpCmdRun","ccmsetup","choco") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the host — confirm explorer.exe→cmd.exe /c→certutil→cmd.exe /K→powershell.exe and inspect the decoded .cmd content and the PowerShell command line for the staging IP 2.26.252.84. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the powershell/cmd chain, and capture the dropped .cmd and any files written to Temp/Public. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same user's mailbox for the 'Case Documents' lure and check other hosts for certutil -decode + outbound to 2.26.252.84 / 45.158.196.184.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "certutil.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "decode"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".cmd"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe"
| where CommandLine has "decode" and CommandLine has ".cmd"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 6f2c1a44-7e0b-4d3a-9a6c-2b91e5d8c401
description: Detects certutil.exe decoding a base64 payload into a .cmd file spawned from cmd.exe/explorer.exe, the HollowFrame LNK delivery step.

logsource:

detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\certutil.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'decode'
      - '.cmd'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\explorer.exe'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe OR *\CERTUTIL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*decode*) @CommandLine:(*.cmd*) @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\explorer.exe OR *\EXPLORER.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\certutil\.exe$/i
| regex("decode", field=CommandLine)
| regex("\.cmd", field=CommandLine)
| ParentBaseFileName=/(cmd|explorer)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

HollowFrame staging server download (PowerShell fetch from 2.26.252.84) AIDelivery Medium
Alerts on any endpoint egress to the HollowFrame next-stage staging host 2.26.252.84, or a PowerShell command line referencing that IP. This is the payload-retrieval step after the LNK/certutil chain and uses a hardcoded article IOC. Rationale: 2.26.252.84 is the article's explicitly named PowerShell fetch/staging IP; direct IOC match on any endpoint egress is high-fidelity delivery evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation VMs deliberately contacting the IOC
  • Security researcher lab traffic
  • Proxy/EDR appliance re-checking the indicator
  • Shared NAT gateway where another benign host reused the IP after takedown
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — expect powershell.exe/cmd.exe descended from explorer→certutil chain; confirm on-host payload artifacts. 2) Contain: block 2.26.252.84 at the egress firewall/proxy and isolate any endpoint that connected. 3) Hunt: sweep for the certutil -decode chain (UC1) and any subsequent connections to 45.158.196.184:8888 and github.com/adioziaete/memio.

| where RemoteIP == "2.26.252.84"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "2.26.252.84"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HollowFrame DLL side-load: python.exe loading rogue python311.dll from user-writable path AIInstallation High
Hunts the HollowFrame loader's signed-binary side-load pair — legitimate python.exe loading a malicious python311.dll from a non-standard, user-writable directory (Temp, Public, AppData\Roaming, ProgramData) rather than a real Python install root. Rationale: Uses the article's exact side-load pair python.exe + python311.dll and constrains to user-writable directories to separate the HollowFrame drop from real Python installs; corroborated by a public Joe Sandbox python311.dll analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html • https://www.joesandbox.com/analysis/1651022/2/html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1055
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/embedded Python bundles shipped inside app folders under ProgramData
  • Developer venv or PyInstaller onedir builds unpacked to Temp
  • Data-science tooling running python from a Downloads folder
  • Vendor agents embedding a private Python runtime outside Program Files
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Anaconda3\", @"\miniconda3\", @"\venv\", @"\.venv\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash python311.dll and check reputation/signing; a Rust/Go-linked or unsigned python311.dll next to python.exe in Temp is malicious. 2) Contain: isolate host, quarantine the DLL + python.exe copy, and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on side-load (version.dll/wtsapi32.dll), scheduled-task persistence, and C2 to 45.158.196.184:8888 or GitHub adioziaete/memio.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "python.exe"
| where FileName =~ "python311.dll"
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Programs\Python", @"\Program Files\Python", @"\Program Files (x86)\Python", @"\WindowsApps\"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Downloads\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Matryoshka side-load: version.dll / wtsapi32.dll loaded from outside System32 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Matryoshka backdoor's side-loaded proxy DLLs — version.dll and wtsapi32.dll — being loaded from any directory outside C:\Windows\System32/SysWOW64/WinSxS. These are genuine Windows library names abused via search-order hijack to run the Rust backdoor. Rationale: version.dll and wtsapi32.dll are the exact Matryoshka side-load DLL names in the article; constraining to loads outside Windows system directories isolates search-order hijack from legitimate OS use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit third-party apps that ship their own version.dll/wtsapi32.dll in their install directory (common for games/media apps)
  • Portable applications run from USB/Downloads
  • Software installers staging DLLs in Temp before moving to Program Files
  • Developer build outputs containing copied system DLLs
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Downloads\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the DLL's signer and the host process — an unsigned version.dll/wtsapi32.dll in Temp/AppData loaded by a non-OS binary is the Matryoshka indicator; hash and detonate. 2) Contain: isolate the host and quarantine the DLL + its loader. 3) Hunt: correlate with the python311.dll side-load (UC3), scheduled-task persistence, and outbound to 45.158.196.184:8888 or api.github.com for adioziaete/memio.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("version.dll","wtsapi32.dll")
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Windows\WinSxS\"))
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Matryoshka HTTP C2 beacon to 45.158.196.184:8888 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on endpoint egress to the Matryoshka backdoor's hardcoded HTTP C2 endpoint 45.158.196.184 on TCP 8888, used by the version.dll variant to spawn a shell and deliver tooling. Uses a fixed IP+port article IOC. Rationale: 45.158.196.184:8888 is the article's explicit Matryoshka HTTP C2 endpoint; a fixed IP+non-standard-port pair is high-confidence C2 evidence with negligible benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/lab detonation of the sample
  • Threat-intel appliance validating the IOC
  • Reuse of the IP by a benign service post-takedown
  • Internal proxy re-checking indicator reputation
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess connecting to 45.158.196.184:8888 — expect a version.dll-hosting signed binary or python.exe; capture the process tree back to the LNK chain. 2) Contain: block the IP at egress, isolate the host, and terminate the beaconing process. 3) Hunt: enumerate AD reconnaissance activity (net/nltest/ldap), scheduled-task persistence, and GitHub C2 to adioziaete/memio on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.158.196.184" and RemotePort == 8888
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "45.158.196.184" and DstPortNumber == 8888
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Matryoshka GitHub C2: non-browser process polling api.github.com / raw.githubusercontent.com AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Matryoshka wtsapi32.dll variant that uses a private GitHub repo (adioziaete/memio) as C2 — beacon.json/cmd.json/result.json per-host mailboxes. Since traffic is HTTPS, this surfaces unexpected, non-developer processes (python.exe, rundll32, or side-loaded DLL hosts) reaching GitHub API/raw endpoints. Rationale: Article names the private GitHub repo adioziaete/memio and the beacon.json/cmd.json/result.json mailbox structure as C2; HTTPS hides the path, so the detectable pivot is unusual non-dev processes reaching GitHub API/raw hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hollowframe-loader-deploys-matryoshka.html
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package managers (pip, npm, go) pulling from raw.githubusercontent.com
  • Update frameworks/agents fetching release assets from GitHub
  • Custom internal automation scripts using the GitHub API
  • Security tooling downloading rule/signature updates from GitHub
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","npm.exe","go.exe","node.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the initiating binary — an unsigned or side-loaded host (python.exe from Temp, or a version.dll/wtsapi32.dll host) polling GitHub on a fixed cadence is the Matryoshka mailbox beacon; check the account adioziaete and repo memio if visible. 2) Contain: block GitHub egress for the offending process/host, isolate the endpoint. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host with the LNK/certutil chain, python311.dll side-load, and 45.158.196.184:8888; review per-host <computer>_<username> directories in the repo history if access is available.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com","codeload.github.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git.exe","code.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","gh.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","devenv.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable Pterodactyl Wings node (< v1.12.3) exposed to CVE-2026-52855 config-secret disclosure
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Pterodactyl Wings daemon-token file (/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml) read by non-Wings process
Vulnerable Pterodactyl Wings node (< v1.12.3) exposed to CVE-2026-52855 config-secret disclosure AIExploitation High
Surfaces hosts running Pterodactyl Wings below v1.12.3, which exposes the full daemon config (including the node daemon token, token_id and docker.registries credentials) to egg configuration-file templating. A low-privileged server owner can smuggle a {{config.token}} placeholder and read the node's daemon token, enabling full-node compromise. This is asset-exposure triage, not a behavioural signature. Rationale: Keys on the article's two concrete disclosure values: the fixed version boundary v1.12.3 and CVE-2026-52855 for the go package github.com/pterodactyl/wings. Confirmed the node token / token_id / docker.registries live in config.yml via pkg.go.dev and the Wings config docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pfvc-3p5h-x7h6 • https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/pterodactyl/wings/config • https://pterodactyl-wings.mintlify.app/configuration/config-file
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Decommissioned/offline nodes still present in stale software inventory
  • Isolated single-tenant nodes where no untrusted user can set egg variables (still vulnerable but lower real risk)
  • Nodes already patched to 1.12.3+ but scanner data not yet refreshed
  • Lab/staging Wings instances intentionally kept on old versions
  • Custom-forked wings builds whose version string does not follow semver and mis-parses
Suppression filter
| where OSPlatform in~ ("Linux")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Wings version on the node (`wings --version`) and whether it is multi-tenant / shared-hosting (untrusted users can set egg variables) — those are the exposed ones. 2) Contain: upgrade Wings to v1.12.3+, then per the advisory rotate the node daemon token (Admin -> Nodes -> Configuration -> reset token) and re-deploy config.yml, since a previously exfiltrated token stays valid until rotated. 3) Hunt: review the node's server volumes and SFTP/file-manager access logs for prior reads of rendered config files, and pivot to UC-2 for any process that touched /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "wings" and (SoftwareVendor has "pterodactyl" or SoftwareName has "pterodactyl")
| extend ParsedVer = parse_version(SoftwareVersion)
| where ParsedVer < parse_version("1.12.3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-52855" or (SoftwareName has "wings" and SoftwareVendor has "pterodactyl")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

Pterodactyl Wings daemon-token file (/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml) read by non-Wings process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts hands-on-keyboard theft of the exact secrets CVE-2026-52855 discloses — the daemon token, token_id and docker.registries stored in /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml. Any process other than the wings daemon that cats, copies, greps or archives this file is high-signal for credential theft on a compromised node. Companion to the version-exposure UC; the templating exfil itself is content-only and not visible in host telemetry. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete secret store: /etc/pterodactyl/config.yml holds config.token (daemon token + JWT HMAC key), config.token_id and config.docker.registries. Confirmed this exact path via the Wings config docs and pkg.go.dev config package. Excludes the legitimate wings daemon to isolate theft. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pfvc-3p5h-x7h6 • https://pterodactyl-wings.mintlify.app/configuration/config-file • https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/pterodactyl/wings/config
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1078
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator manually inspecting config.yml during maintenance (cat/less/vim)
  • Backup or archival jobs (tar/rsync/cp of /etc/pterodactyl) sweeping the config
  • Configuration-management runs (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) templating or reading config.yml
  • Monitoring/inventory agents fingerprinting installed software
  • Wings upgrade/reinstall scripts copying the config to a backup before rewrite
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tar","rsync","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","cp") and FileName !in~ ("tar","rsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the reading process, user, and parent — was it an interactive shell (attacker) or a known backup/config-mgmt daemon? Check the account against expected node admins. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the node, rotate the daemon token (Admin -> Nodes -> reset token, re-deploy config.yml) and any docker registry credentials it referenced, and revoke active Wings JWTs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for other server volumes accessed, SFTP downloads of rendered config files, and outbound use of the token against the Panel<->Wings API on other servers of that node.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml"
| where FileName !in~ ("wings")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/etc/pterodactyl/config.yml"
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "/wings" and ActingProcessName !~ "wings"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Anthropic's Fever Dream: Claude's package that stole real keys
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious 'anthropickit' PyPI package installed via pip (supply-chain cred stealer) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] anthropickit loot file '/tmp/runner_exfil.json' written to disk · [LLM] anthropickit exfiltration POST to Pipedream endpoint (enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream.net)
Malicious 'anthropickit' PyPI package installed via pip (supply-chain cred stealer) AIInstallation High
Hunts pip/python installing the specific malicious package 'anthropickit' whose setup.py steals SSH keys and CI secrets at install time. Targets the exact package name (dependency-confusion sentinel v999.9.9) rather than a generic pip-install template. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package name 'anthropickit' (confirmed by OSV MAL-2026-904 and CIRCL MAL-2026-5755) combined with a pip/python execution context; the name is unique enough that any hit is the malicious package, not a false positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/anthropic-rogue-agents-package-stole-keys • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-904 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-5755 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/anthropic-says-claude-mistook-open.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally testing/reverse-engineering the malware sample in a sandbox
  • Security-vendor package scanners that install-and-detonate PyPI packages (this is exactly how one victim in the article was hit — treat as TP unless known scanner infra)
  • Internal wiki/ticket automation echoing the package name into a shell command that never actually installs it
  • A benign internal package deliberately named 'anthropickit' (none known to exist)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !in~ ("malware-analysis-01","pkg-scanner-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually ran 'pip install anthropickit' vs. merely referencing the string; pull the full process tree and the invoking user/CI job. 2) Contain: kill the CI runner / isolate the host, rotate ALL SSH private keys under the affected identity and every env-var secret matching KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASS/AUTH/API, and revoke associated cloud/API tokens — assume full compromise the instant install ran. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for /tmp/runner_exfil.json and outbound connections to pipedream.net from the same hosts (see companion UCs); pivot on the same PyPI account/mirror config to find other pulled packages.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit"
| where FileName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","-m pip")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "anthropickit"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("pip","python") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","setup.py","-m pip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

anthropickit loot file '/tmp/runner_exfil.json' written to disk AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the exact loot file the anthropickit stealer writes before exfiltration, containing harvested SSH keys and CI secrets. Near-zero-FP file artifact unique to this malware ('runner_exfil.json' in /tmp). Rationale: The filename 'runner_exfil.json' in /tmp is a hardcoded, unique artifact of this specific stealer (verified in the setup.py sample and CIRCL/OSV writeups); its presence is effectively pathognomonic and needs no threshold. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/anthropic-rogue-agents-package-stole-keys • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-5755 • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-904
ATT&CKT1005 T1074.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysts detonating the sample in a lab (file will legitimately appear)
  • An IR/forensics playbook that copies the recovered loot file back to /tmp on a test box
  • A coincidentally-named internal script writing runner_exfil.json (no legitimate tool is known to use this name)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture and hash the file, note the writing process (should be python/pip); the JSON contents reveal exactly which SSH keys and env secrets were harvested. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate every credential enumerated in the file plus all SSH private keys for the identity; delete the file only after evidence capture. 3) Hunt: correlate with 'pip install anthropickit' execution and outbound pipedream.net traffic on the same host; sweep all CI runners sharing the same base image or secret store.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "runner_exfil.json" or FolderPath has "/tmp/runner_exfil.json"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "runner_exfil.json" or TargetFilePath has "runner_exfil.json"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

anthropickit exfiltration POST to Pipedream endpoint (enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream.net) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the outbound exfiltration channel used by anthropickit — a python/pip process reaching a Pipedream webhook to POST stolen SSH keys and CI secrets. Anchors on the specific IOC host and the broader python→pipedream.net pattern. Rationale: Uses the exact hardcoded exfil host enqqnvvtgrnyl.x.pipedream.net (high-fidelity IOC in Sigma) plus the durable python/pip→pipedream.net pattern for endpoints where the specific throwaway URL has rotated; process context suppresses benign developer Pipedream use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/anthropic-rogue-agents-package-stole-keys • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/mal-2026-5755 • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/MAL-2026-904 • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/anthropics-claude-breached-3-orgs-uploaded-pypi-malware-during-tests/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately using Pipedream workflow webhooks from python scripts (broad pipedream.net clause — the exact IOC host clause has no legit use)
  • Python-based monitoring/CI integrations that POST to pipedream.net endpoints
  • A requests-based app whose parent is python but is unrelated to the stealer
  • Package scanners detonating the sample and generating the beacon
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "pipedream.net" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("webhook","scheduled-job") and DeviceName in~ ("ci-integration-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the destination is the exact IOC host (definitive TP) or generic pipedream.net (verify against a known-good Pipedream allowlist); pull the initiating process and command line. 2) Contain: block pipedream.net at egress for CI/build ranges, isolate the host, and rotate all SSH keys and secrets — the POST body is the exfiltrated credential set. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for 'pip install anthropickit' and /tmp/runner_exfil.json; review the PyPI/mirror config to identify what else was pulled and which secrets store the runner could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "pipedream.net" or RemoteUrl has "enqqnvvtgrnyl"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","pip","pip3") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.py","pip install")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "pipedream.net"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:

            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or SHA1 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or MD5 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or SHA1 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc") or MD5 in~ ("4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["4ae13303fa1663a36cfaa70bebe77b52b12dbf17eef24db15c6c24c631d38fbf", "f3e103a8a230b5fb3066fb0a9eb7f5fdf5831d4c7b71a9d83de54d8d6673eae2", "ff4126bd465ae6de09a2eaa94a4fd2d7d385a5dae2c093372668d4b7ecb81633", "584ef638a5415f4eccf6645abbcd06198e9abecf8b75cbd9328aa58962d9b38b", "7df12487bade710459ccea2d3570cdbc"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cheap Android TV Boxes Pose as Phones and Turn Owners’ Broadband Into Proxies

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 8 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Bitsight says some cheap Android TV boxes have shipped with apps that rewrite their hardware identity to mimic Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi, or Vivo phones, then click ads on websites run by the same operators. Researchers named the operation Fuyao and attributed it to Zhejiang Fengwo IoT Technology Co., Ltd., a mainland China company founded in 2019. The same apps have a second job. When a box

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Fuyao Android TV-box botnet C2/backdoor egress to fwgcloud.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Fuyao Android TV-box botnet C2/backdoor egress to fwgcloud.com AICommand & Control Medium
Surfaces any host or on-network device resolving or connecting to fwgcloud.com, the expired-then-sinkholed domain Bitsight identified as the Fuyao operation's factory backdoor and telemetry collector. Article-specific because it anchors on the single confirmed network indicator tied to the Zhejiang Fengwo 'Fuyao' Android-TV-box ad-fraud / SOCKS5 residential-proxy botnet, not generic beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on fwgcloud.com — the single confirmed Fuyao network indicator, which Bitsight uncovered by registering the expired domain and using it as a sinkhole/factory-backdoor collector. Any enterprise host or managed device resolving it indicates a Fuyao-infected TV box or a related implant on the network. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cheap-android-tv-boxes-pose-as-phones.html • https://www.bitsight.com/blog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security-tooling / sinkhole or threat-intel appliance deliberately resolving fwgcloud.com for enrichment
  • A researcher or analyst manually browsing to the domain during triage
  • Passive-DNS or DNS-logging collectors replaying historical queries into the SIEM
  • Typo-squat or unrelated benign subdomain that happens to end in the same string (low likelihood given full-domain anchor)
Suppression filter
| where Computer !in~ ("sinkhole-collector01", "ti-enrichment01") and ClientProc !in~ ("threatintel.exe", "dnscollector.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the resolving/connecting asset via DeviceName/ClientIP; determine whether it is a managed endpoint or an unmanaged IoT/Android device on guest/corporate VLAN. Correlate the initiating process and any HDMI-linked network segment. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block fwgcloud.com at DNS and egress firewall; quarantine or network-isolate the offending device (per FBI June-2025 guidance, disconnect suspect streaming boxes). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP for SOCKS5-style outbound relaying, ad-domain callbacks to any of Bitsight's 144 operator domains, S3 fetches of JavaScript fraud modules, and spoofed device-identifier (Samsung/Huawei/Xiaomi/Vivo) beacons from the same NAT/segment.
let c2domain = "fwgcloud.com";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where RemoteUrl has c2domain
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ClientProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, SrcTable = "DeviceNetworkEvents"),
  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
   | where AdditionalFields has c2domain or RemoteUrl has c2domain
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ClientProc = InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort = int(null), SrcTable = "DeviceEvents-DNS")
| order by Timestamp desc
let c2domain = "fwgcloud.com";
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name has c2domain
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Domain = Name, SrcTable = "DnsEvents"),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has c2domain
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Domain = DnsQuery, SrcTable = "ImDnsActivity"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has c2domain or RequestURL has c2domain or DestinationDnsDomain has c2domain
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Domain = coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationDnsDomain, RequestURL), SrcTable = "CommonSecurityLog")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

level: high

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.record_type) as record_type from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*fwgcloud.com" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest index sourcetype | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="*fwgcloud.com" OR All_Traffic.url="*fwgcloud.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.record_type) as record_type from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*fwgcloud.com" by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest index sourcetype | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)` | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="*fwgcloud.com" OR All_Traffic.url="*fwgcloud.com") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("") or RemoteUrl has_any ("fwgcloud.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic([""]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["fwgcloud.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("fwgcloud.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("fwgcloud.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("fwgcloud.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("fwgcloud.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 13 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Device code phishing - the abuse of the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant to steal access tokens - has evolved from a niche red-team technique to an industrial-scale threat in under six months. Designed for input-constrained devices like smart TVs, printers, and so on, the device authorization login flow has been adopted by a wide range of apps and use-cases that it wasn't originally
