Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phishing email delivering a device-code login portal link (devicelogin / oauth2 deviceauth) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Successful OAuth 2.0 device code grant from country never seen for the user · [LLM] Device-code flow requested for an unexpected public client application · [LLM] Geographic impossibility between device-code entry and token redemption · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Device registration / PRT theft via Microsoft Authentication Broker after device code sign-in
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Anomalous device code authentication request pattern from risky/anonymized source
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Cloud lateral movement via a compromised device-code token (multi-service fan-out) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Successful OAuth 2.0 device code grant from country never seen for the user AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant (device code flow) from a country the user has never signed in from — the core Storm-2372/EvilTokens technique where Microsoft issues a token to the attacker's polling client after the victim approves a code. Device-code auth is rare in most tenants, so a first-seen-country device-code success is high-signal. Rationale: Uses the article's core mechanic — a successful device-code grant issuing a token to the attacker — plus a per-user first-seen-country anti-join to strip legitimate device-code use. Microsoft's Storm-2372 write-up and Silverfort confirm device-code sign-ins carry authenticationProtocol=deviceCode; where that column is unavailable this pivots on AuthenticationProcessingDetails. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://www.silverfort.com/blog/device-code-attacks-in-azure-from-exploitation-to-detection/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traveling employee legitimately using az login / Azure PowerShell device code abroad for the first time
  • New IoT/kiosk enrollment via device code from a branch office in a new country
  • Road-warrior developer using VS Code tunnels / GitHub CLI device flow from a new location
  • Corporate VPN egress that geolocates to a country the user hasn't used before
Suppression filter
| where UserPrincipalName !in~ ("svc-kiosk@contoso.com", "iot-enroll@contoso.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the org uses device-code flow at all; check the sign-in IP/ASN/UserAgent and whether the user has a concurrent interactive sign-in from their normal geo (indicates attacker redeemed while victim was elsewhere). 2) Contain: revoke the user's sessions and refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), force password reset + re-registration of MFA, and apply/verify a Conditional Access policy blocking device-code flow for non-exempt users. 3) Hunt: pivot the user into the device-registration/PRT UC and the mailbox/SharePoint fan-out UC to detect persistence and collection.

Device registration / PRT theft via Microsoft Authentication Broker after device code sign-in AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a successful device-code sign-in with a subsequent Entra 'Add/Register device' by the same user via the Microsoft Authentication Broker app (29d9ed98-...), the PRT-persistence chain kits like ARToken use to register an attacker device and mint self-renewing Primary Refresh Tokens that survive password resets. Rationale: Ties the article's PRT-persistence claim (ARToken ships with PRT persistence) to concrete telemetry: a deviceCode sign-in to the Microsoft Authentication Broker app (appId 29d9ed98-...) immediately followed by a first-seen device registration isolates attacker PRT setup from routine Intune enrollment. Sigma skipped — cross-table (SigninLogs x AuditLogs) correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Intune/Autopilot enrollment right after a legitimate device-code login on a new corporate laptop
  • BYOD registration by a remote user from a home/mobile IP
  • Identity admin bulk-registering devices during a migration
  • Windows Hello for Business provisioning registering the device
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in ("<corp-egress-ip-1>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the newly registered device's join IP/country and device name against the user's baseline and corporate naming; confirm a device-code broker sign-in preceded it. 2) Contain: delete the rogue device object in Entra, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, and reset credentials (a PRT survives password reset alone, so token revocation is mandatory). 3) Hunt: enumerate all devices registered by finance/AP users in the window from the same IP and pivot to inbox-rule creation and bulk SharePoint/mailbox access from that actor.

Anomalous device code authentication request pattern from risky/anonymized source AICommand & Control Medium
Flags successful device-code sign-ins originating from anonymous proxies/VPN/TOR or scored risky by Identity Protection, then fanning out to high-sensitivity resources (Exchange Online, SharePoint, Graph, Teams) shortly after — the post-approval behaviour where a stolen device-code token is immediately used against mail and files. Rationale: Combines the article's 'token stolen then used for mailbox/SharePoint access' narrative with Identity Protection risk/anonymized-source signals; the Sentinel variant correlates the device-code grant to a same-user fan-out across sensitive resources within an hour to raise fidelity above a bare device-code alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/device-code-phishing

Phishing email delivering a device-code login portal link (devicelogin / oauth2 deviceauth) AIDelivery Medium
Detects inbound delivered email whose embedded URL points to a legitimate device-authorization portal (microsoft.com/devicelogin, /oauth2/deviceauth, github.com/login/device, AWS SSO device endpoints) and correlates a click within 10 minutes — the initial-access lure that steers a victim to enter the attacker's short code on the real provider page. Rationale: The article states device-code lures are delivered through email and other channels and route users to the provider's legitimate device-login page; keying on inbound-delivered mail whose URL is a device-authorization portal (not a cloned login page) captures the article's specific delivery vector, distinct from generic link+exec. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon left empty because per-message URL and Safe Links click telemetry (EmailUrlInfo/UrlClickEvents) has no clean equivalent in those platforms in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/device-code-phishing
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate IT onboarding email instructing users to complete a device-code login for a new device/CLI tool
  • Vendor/SaaS notification containing a genuine github.com/login/device or AWS SSO link
  • Security-awareness simulation using a device-code lure
  • Newsletter/advisory that quotes microsoft.com/devicelogin as text in an email body
Suppression filter
| where SenderMailFromDomain !in~ ("it-helpdesk.contoso.com", "yourphishingsimvendor.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify sender domain/authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) and whether the message impersonates IT/helpdesk; confirm DeliveryAction and whether a click occurred. 2) Contain: ZAP/purge the message from all recipient mailboxes, block the sender, and warn any user who clicked; check that user for a subsequent device-code sign-in. 3) Hunt: search all mailboxes for the same device-code URL pattern and pivot every clicker into the successful device-code grant UC.
let Window = 10m;
let DeviceCodeUrls = dynamic(["microsoft.com/devicelogin", "oauth2/deviceauth", "github.com/login/device", "aka.ms/devicelogin", "device.sso", "login.microsoftonline.com/common/oauth2/deviceauth"]);
let PhishMail = EmailEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
    | join kind=inner (EmailUrlInfo | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | project NetworkMessageId, Url) on NetworkMessageId
    | where Url has_any (DeviceCodeUrls)
    | project MailTime = Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url;
PhishMail
| join kind=inner (
    UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed", "ClickedThrough")
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, AccountUpn, IPAddress
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| where ClickTime between (MailTime .. MailTime + Window)
| project MailTime, ClickTime, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, AccountUpn, Subject, Url, IPAddress
| order by ClickTime desc

Cloud lateral movement via a compromised device-code token (multi-service fan-out) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a stolen device-code token pivoting across the tenant: after a device-code grant, the same user/IP authenticates non-interactively to four or more distinct cloud services (Exchange, SharePoint, Teams, Graph, Dynamics) or drives bulk enumeration — the SSO-level fan-out that turns one app grant into tenant-wide access. Rationale: Maps the article's 'privilege escalation from a stolen token to full SSO-level access' to a same-token/same-IP fan-out across distinct cloud resources within 6h of the device-code grant; the dcount threshold distinguishes tenant-wide pivoting from normal single-app use. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon empty — multi-table threshold correlation on Azure identity telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/analyzing-the-instructure-breach
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A power user legitimately working across Exchange, SharePoint, Teams and Graph in one session
  • First-day setup where a client silently authenticates to many services
  • Shared NAT/egress IP causing multiple users' resources to collapse onto one IP
  • Automation/service principal touching several APIs behind one token
Suppression filter
| where DcIP !in ("<corp-egress-ip-1>", "<corp-vpn-egress-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the fan-out followed a device-code grant and originates from an anomalous IP/geo; list the resources and any bulk enumeration (mailbox search, file listing, directory queries). 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens, disable the account if active theft is confirmed, and block device-code flow via Conditional Access. 3) Hunt: correlate to bulk SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, inbox-rule creation, and outbound BEC from the same account across the tenant.
let DeviceCode = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode" and ErrorCode == 0
    | project DcTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, DcIP = IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| join kind=inner DeviceCode on $left.IPAddress == $right.DcIP
| where Timestamp between (DcTime .. DcTime + 6h)
| summarize Apps = dcount(Application), Actions = count(), SampleActions = make_set(ActionType, 15), Services = make_set(Application, 20) by AccountUpn, DcIP, DcTime
| where Apps >= 3   // token driving activity across 3+ distinct cloud apps from the redemption IP
| order by DcTime desc
let DeviceCode = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode"
    | where ResultType == 0
    | project DcTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, DcIP = IPAddress;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=inner DeviceCode on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (DcTime .. DcTime + 6h)
| where IPAddress == DcIP   // same redemption client/IP as the device-code grant
| summarize DistinctResources = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 20), Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 20) by UserPrincipalName, DcIP, DcTime
| where DistinctResources >= 4   // SSO-level fan-out across 4+ distinct resources
| order by DcTime desc

Device-code flow requested for an unexpected public client application AIExploitation Medium
Flags device-code sign-ins targeting consumer/CLI first-party client IDs that most tenants never legitimately drive via device code (Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Microsoft Office, Authentication Broker, VS Code) — a telltale misuse signature when device code is used to phish tokens for broadly-scoped clients rather than genuine constrained devices. Rationale: Targets the article's point that device code exists for constrained devices but is abused for broadly-scoped clients; scoping to well-known first-party public client IDs (Azure CLI/PowerShell/Office/Auth Broker/VS Code) used with device code flags the misuse signature. Falcon/CloudWatch empty — Azure sign-in telemetry not in FDR/CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://pushsecurity.com/blog/device-code-phishing

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • VS Code Remote/tunnels device-code sign-ins by engineers
  • Admins using device code for Office activation on shared devices
  • CI/CD or automation that legitimately uses device_code against Azure CLI
Suppression filter
| where UserPrincipalName !in~ ("devops@contoso.com", "svc-ci@contoso.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the user is an engineer/admin who legitimately uses CLI device-code auth and whether the source IP/geo/UserAgent matches their baseline. 2) Contain: for anomalous cases revoke tokens, reset credentials, and consider a Conditional Access policy scoping device-code flow to only approved user groups/clients. 3) Hunt: pivot flagged users into the first-seen-country device-code UC and device-registration UC.

Geographic impossibility between device-code entry and token redemption AIExploitation Medium
Correlates a device-code sign-in with the same user's interactive sign-in within a short window and flags when the device-code redemption country differs from where the user is actually signing in — exposing an attacker redeeming the stolen code from a different geo than the victim who entered it. Rationale: Operationalizes the article's structural point that identity proof (victim, one geo) and authorization grant (attacker, another geo) are separate: a device-code redemption whose country differs from the same user's near-simultaneous interactive sign-in isolates the split-geo signature of a stolen code. Sigma/Datadog/Falcon empty — cross-event geo correlation on Azure identity telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://www.silverfort.com/blog/device-code-attacks-in-azure-from-exploitation-to-detection/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User on a VPN whose interactive session egresses in a different country than the device-code client
  • Legitimate device-code login on a remote/cloud VM in another region while the user works locally
  • Mobile roaming causing geo split between two of the user's sessions
  • Geo-IP inaccuracy placing two same-user sessions in adjacent-but-different countries
Suppression filter
| where DeviceCodeIP !in ("<corp-vpn-egress-ip>") and UserIP !in ("<corp-vpn-egress-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the two sessions belong to the same user and rule out VPN/remote-VM by inspecting both IPs/ASNs; the interactive geo is likely the real user, the device-code geo the attacker. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens, reset credentials, and block device-code flow via Conditional Access for the user. 3) Hunt: pivot the device-code IP into device-registration, resource fan-out, and inbox-rule UCs, and check for other users redeemed from the same attacker IP/ASN.
let Window = 30m;
let Interactive = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | where not(AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode")
    | project IntTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, UserCountry = Country, UserIP = IPAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode" and ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=inner Interactive on AccountUpn
| where IntTime between (Timestamp - Window .. Timestamp + Window)
| where isnotempty(Country) and isnotempty(UserCountry) and Country != UserCountry
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, DeviceCodeCountry = Country, DeviceCodeIP = IPAddress, UserCountry, UserIP, IntTime
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 30m;
let Interactive = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0 and IsInteractive == true
    | where not(AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode")
    | extend UserCtry = tostring(parse_json(LocationDetails).countryOrRegion)
    | project IntTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserCtry, UserIP = IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode" and ResultType == 0
| extend DcCtry = tostring(parse_json(LocationDetails).countryOrRegion)
| join kind=inner Interactive on UserPrincipalName
| where IntTime between (TimeGenerated - Window .. TimeGenerated + Window)
| where isnotempty(DcCtry) and isnotempty(UserCtry) and DcCtry != UserCtry
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, DeviceCodeCountry = DcCtry, DeviceCodeIP = IPAddress, UserCountry = UserCtry, UserIP, IntTime
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 12 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 says a Chinese-speaking threat actor used DeepSeek through the open-source Hermes Agent framework to launch attacks autonomously. After an initial Telegram instruction, the agent found internet-facing systems and selected public exploits. The researchers recovered no further operator input in the session. The operator, tracked through the aliases knaithe and KnYuan,

Citrix NetScaler SAML IdP memory-overread scraping loop (CVE-2026-3055) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the one confirmed successful vector in this campaign: automated repeated requests against a NetScaler ADC/Gateway configured as a SAML IdP to bleed session data/credentials from memory (CVE-2026-3055). Article + Unit 42 confirm data exfiltration from three orgs via this flaw; the memory-overread has to be looped to collect useful bytes, producing a request burst against the SAML IdP endpoint. Rationale: Uses the confirmed precondition (NetScaler configured as SAML IdP, `add authentication samlIdPProfile`) and the memory-overread mechanic (looped requests + oversized responses) that Citrix/Rapid7 and Unit 42 describe, rather than a generic web-exploit template. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-3055-citrix-netscaler-adc-and-netscaler-gateway-out-of-bounds-read/ • https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-006-vulnerability-impacting-citrix-netscaler-adc-netscaler-gateway-cve-2026-3055
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SAML SSO burst during an SP-initiated login storm (e.g. morning logon peak or an outage recovery)
  • SAML metadata refresh / federation health-check probes from a partner IdP-SP
  • Vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable/watchTowr) fingerprinting the SAML IdP endpoint
  • Load balancer or synthetic monitoring hitting the SSO URL on a short interval
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["<known_SP_or_partner_IdP_ranges_via_watchlist>"]))  // maintain as a Sentinel watchlist of legitimate SAML SP/IdP source IPs
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationHostName is a NetScaler with a SAML IdP profile configured; check whether the SourceIP is a known SP/partner IdP or an unknown internet host, and look at response sizes for abnormal growth. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter and apply the fixed NetScaler build from Citrix's bulletin; if SAML IdP is not required, remove the profile. 3) Hunt: rotate all SAML/session secrets and force re-auth for exposed users, then pivot on the same SourceIP across other appliances and correlate with any Marimo command-exec or Telegram/DeepSeek egress from the same window.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor has "Citrix" or DeviceProduct has_any ("NetScaler","ADC","Gateway")
| where RequestURL has "saml"
| summarize Requests=count(), MaxRespBytes=max(toreal(SentBytes)), TotalRespBytes=sum(toreal(SentBytes)), SampleUris=make_set(RequestURL,8) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where Requests > 20   // >20 SAML IdP hits/10m from one src = memory-overread scraping loop, not a normal SSO login
| order by TotalRespBytes desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as requests, max(Web.bytes_out) as max_bytes_out, values(Web.uri_path) as uris from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.dest_category="netscaler" OR Web.dest="*netscaler*" OR Web.http_user_agent="*") Web.uri_path="*saml*" by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where requests>20 | sort - max_bytes_out
| tstats summariesonly=false count as requests, max(Web.bytes_out) as max_bytes_out, values(Web.uri_path) as uris from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.dest_category="netscaler" OR Web.dest="*netscaler*" OR Web.http_user_agent="*") Web.uri_path="*saml*" by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where requests>20 | sort - max_bytes_out
Marimo notebook server spawning shell/downloader (CVE-2026-39987 command execution) AIInstallation High
Hunts the confirmed command-execution vector against internet-exposed Marimo notebook instances (CVE-2026-39987, 11 instances hit). Detects the Marimo (python) server process spawning a shell/downloader/reverse-shell child — the on-host footprint of exploitation, distinct from the inbound web request. Rationale: Anchors on the named product+CVE (Marimo, CVE-2026-39987, fixed in 0.23.0) and the confirmed 11-instance command execution, expressed as the notebook-server→shell process tree rather than a generic 'python spawns bash' rule. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientist legitimately running shell/`!pip install`/`curl` cells inside an authenticated Marimo notebook
  • CI/automation launching Marimo and shelling out to fetch datasets
  • A Marimo app that legitimately calls curl/wget to hydrate remote data on startup
  • Internal red-team validating the patch state of Marimo
Suppression filter
| where not (ActorUsername in~ ("datascience-svc","ci-runner") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","pip3 install"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Marimo instance is internet-exposed and its version is <0.23.0; inspect the child command line for reverse-shell (`/dev/tcp`, `bash -i`) or payload download vs. a benign notebook cell. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Marimo process, and restrict the notebook interface to authenticated/internal access; patch to Marimo 0.23.0. 3) Hunt: pull outbound connections from the child process, check for `python3 -m http.server 8888` staging and Telegram/DeepSeek egress on the same host, and review auditd for follow-on persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")) or (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","python3") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-i","/dev/tcp","curl","wget","base64","| sh","| bash","socket"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess=FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "marimo"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-i","/dev/tcp","curl","wget","base64","| sh","| bash") or ActingProcessName in~ ("curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Marimo Notebook Server Spawning Shell or Downloader (CVE-2026-39987)
id: 3f2b6c7a-9d41-4e88-b6a2-1c5e0f7a8b21
description: Detects a Marimo notebook server (python) spawning a shell, downloader or reverse-shell child, consistent with CVE-2026-39987 command execution.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/chinese-hacker-commands-deepseek-via.html
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentCommandLine|contains: 'marimo'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
  selection_intent:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/dev/tcp'
      - 'bash -i'
      - 'curl '
      - 'wget '
      - 'base64 -d'
  condition: selection_parent and (selection_child or selection_intent)

Hermes Agent opsec tell: python3 -m http.server 8888 staging server AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the exact opsec failure that exposed this operation: the Hermes Agent starting `python3 -m http.server 8888` from /home/worker, which unintentionally published the actor's exploit scripts, target lists, API keys and session logs. On any host in your estate this indicates a Hermes-style autonomous agent staging/exfil directory. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's most specific string — `python3 -m http.server 8888` started from /home/worker — a high-fidelity, non-generic staging indicator confirmed by Unit 42 as the operation's exposure point. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer serving static files locally with `python3 -m http.server 8888` for testing
  • A dev container / tutorial default that binds http.server to 8888
  • Ad-hoc file transfer between admins on an internal host
  • Legacy build script using SimpleHTTPServer on 8888
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("builduser","developer") and FolderPath !startswith "/home/dev"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account and cwd of the http.server process (expect a non-interactive/service account such as 'worker') and list files in the served directory for exploit scripts, target lists, API keys or session logs. 2) Contain: kill the process, block inbound 8888 at the host firewall, and image the served directory for evidence before it is cleaned. 3) Hunt: enumerate what fetched from this server (access pattern), and pivot on the same host for Marimo/NetScaler exploitation activity and Telegram/DeepSeek egress to confirm a Hermes Agent deployment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("http.server","8888")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("http.server","8888")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hermes Agent Staging Server - python http.server on 8888

Hermes Agent Telegram bot C2 egress from a server/notebook workload AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the command-and-control channel described in the article: the Hermes Agent taking operator instructions via the Telegram Bot API. Flags server-side workloads (python/node/curl or the exploited app processes) resolving/connecting to api.telegram.org — abnormal for a Langflow/n8n/Marimo/NetScaler host. Rationale: Encodes the article's core C2 mechanic ('commands DeepSeek via Telegram') as server-workload egress to api.telegram.org — high-fidelity because production Langflow/n8n/Marimo/NetScaler hosts should not be talking to the Telegram Bot API from a shell/python context. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://gbhackers.com/hacker-uses-deepseek-agent/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An n8n workflow that legitimately uses the built-in Telegram node for alerting (very common — tune out known n8n hosts)
  • A monitoring/alerting script that pushes notifications to a Telegram channel
  • DevOps chatops bot sending deploy notifications from a CI host
  • A developer testing a Telegram bot integration on a shared server
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("n8n-prod-01","n8n-prod-02")  // maintain an allowlist of hosts with sanctioned Telegram integrations
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the originating host runs a sanctioned Telegram integration (e.g. an approved n8n Telegram node) vs. an ad-hoc python/curl process; inspect the process command line and parentage. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, block api.telegram.org egress for server subnets, and capture the bot token/process artifacts. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for `http.server 8888` staging, DeepSeek API egress, and Marimo/NetScaler exploitation; extract the bot token to identify the C2 channel.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "telegram.org" or RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","node","curl","wget","sh","bash") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("marimo","n8n","langflow","hermes")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has "api.telegram.org" or RequestURL has "api.telegram.org"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeepSeek LLM inference API egress from an exposed server workload AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the reasoning channel of the Hermes Agent: outbound calls to the DeepSeek inference API from a server/notebook/workflow host. On the estate this is the tell of an autonomous LLM-driven attack agent running locally, distinct from the Telegram command channel and the http.server staging directory. Rationale: Targets the article's central claim (DeepSeek as the Hermes Agent reasoning model) via egress to the documented DeepSeek API host from a server-context process; api.deepseek.com is the verifiable DeepSeek endpoint (not stated in the article), so confidence is deliberately Low and it should be corroborated by the Telegram/http.server UCs on the same host. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/322582/20260801/deepseek-ran-autonomous-cyberattacks-that-claude-openai-safety-controls-blocked.htm
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned internal app/microservice that legitimately calls the DeepSeek API for a product feature
  • Developer experimentation with DeepSeek SDKs on a shared build host
  • An AI gateway/proxy host that brokers LLM calls for the org
  • A data pipeline enriching records via a DeepSeek endpoint
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in ("ai-gateway-01","llm-proxy-01")  // allowlist sanctioned LLM-egress hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether DeepSeek API usage is sanctioned for this host and whether the initiating process is a known app vs. an ad-hoc python/shell process; review the frequency/volume of calls. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host and block LLM-API egress for server subnets, then capture process artifacts and any API keys in the working directory. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for Telegram Bot API egress and `http.server 8888` staging; if all three co-occur, treat as an active Hermes Agent deployment and escalate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "deepseek.com" or RemoteUrl has "api.deepseek.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","node","curl","wget","sh","bash") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("marimo","n8n","langflow","hermes")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has "deepseek.com" or RequestURL has "api.deepseek.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

Network Anomaly Detection in KATA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-31 9 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An analysis of how Network Anomaly Detection (NAD) rules work within Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack, using Kerberoasting and DNS tunneling attacks as examples.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1558 T1558.003
Domainstestinglab.ru crust.testinglab.ru
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
