Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exploited AnySign4PC.exe spawning child process or dropping DLL · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Exploit AnySign4PC via Hacked Korean Sites to Install Backdoors Without
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SIGNBT/Gunra payload staging via net.tmp and inet.tmp · [LLM] COPPERHEDGE/SIGNBT C2 config in service-registry blobs + unusual service creation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) · [LLM] Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anti-forensic evidence destruction: SDelete / CCleaner + 4-char rename-then-delete · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint contact with jshosting[.]me, the domain AhnLab/KISA attribute to distribution of the version-specific AnySign4PC exploit scripts in both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains. Because the exploit runs with no download prompt, the DNS/HTTP callout to this domain is often the earliest host-visible signal of the drive-by. Rationale: jshosting[.]me is a hard IOC confirmed by AhnLab as the exploit-script distribution domain shared by both the espionage and Gunra intrusions; a corporate host resolving it is high-fidelity given it is not a legitimate service. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1189 T1608.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox that egresses through the corporate resolver
  • Threat-intel enrichment/crawler tooling actively resolving IOC domains
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the query as it blocks it (verify answer is sinkhole IP)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the callout — a browser process is consistent with the watering-hole drive-by; confirm the user visited a Korean news/healthcare/education site immediately prior. 2) Contain: block jshosting[.]me at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and snapshot AnySign4PC version (flag 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for AnySign4PC.exe spawning children/writing DLLs, injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe, and outbound to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "jshosting.me" or RemoteUrl endswith ".jshosting.me"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "jshosting.me"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploited AnySign4PC.exe spawning child process or dropping DLL AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation moment where the buffer-overflow in AnySign4PC.exe (Hancom Secure e-signature client) forces the signed process to spawn a child or write a DLL to disk with no user interaction. A certificate-signing client legitimately never spawns interpreters/LOLBins or drops DLLs, so either behaviour from AnySign4PC.exe is anomalous. Rationale: AnySign4PC.exe is the exact exploited binary named by ENKI/KISA; a signing client spawning children or dropping DLLs is behaviourally impossible in benign use, matching Plainbit's 'generated an error and created a malicious DLL without a download prompt'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.enki.co.kr/en/media-center/blog/joint-cybersecurity-advisory-watering-hole-malware-analysis • https://www.file.net/process/anysign4pc.exe.html
ATT&CKT1203 T1055 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AnySign4PC auto-update spawning its own updater/installer (AnySignUpdate.exe)
  • Crash-handler WerFault.exe launched by AnySign4PC after a benign fault
  • Vendor troubleshooting tool bundled with AnySign4PC launching a helper
  • EDR/AV telemetry stub injected into AnySign4PC being recorded as a child
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("AnySignUpdate.exe","AnySignSetup.exe") and not (FileName =~ "WerFault.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-p")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process command line and any dropped DLL path/hash; a LOLBin (rundll32/regsvr32) child or a DLL written to ProgramData/Temp is a strong true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (backdoor decrypts stages in memory and may be disk-absent), and record AnySign4PC version. 3) Hunt: pivot to svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe injection, net.tmp/inet.tmp artifacts, service-registry blobs, and C2 to 176.65.128[.]26 on the same device.
let ProcSpawn = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnySign4PC.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("AnySign4PC.exe","AnySignUpdate.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="ChildProcess", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
let DllDrop = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnySign4PC.exe"
| where ActionType == "FileCreated" and FileName endswith ".dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="DllDrop", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
ProcSpawn | union DllDrop
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\AnySign4PC.exe"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\AnySign4PC.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound connection to 176.65.128[.]26, the reverse-tunnelling address AhnLab confirms was reused across both the state-sponsored SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE chain and the Gunra ransomware chain. Any egress to this fixed IP from a corporate host is a high-confidence compromise indicator. Rationale: 176.65.128[.]26 is a fixed IOC that AhnLab confirms as the reverse-tunnelling address shared across both operations — a rare dual-corroborated hard indicator that warrants direct alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/lazarus-group-exploits-anysign4pc-zero-day-to-target-south-korean-financial-sector-via-drive-by-attacks
ATT&CKT1572 T1071 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel validation traffic or IOC scanner probing the IP from a security appliance
  • Firewall logging the connection as denied (check DeviceAction=blocked before escalating)
  • Shared hosting rebind — verify the IP is still attacker-controlled at alert time
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","nmap.exe") and DeviceName !has "scanner"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe or an unsigned binary reaching this IP is an immediate true positive; note the port (SSH/reverse-tunnel often 22/443). 2) Contain: block the IP org-wide, isolate the host, and preserve volatile memory before the loader's self-protection wipes disk artifacts. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internal hosts that contacted the IP, and on each check for Mimikatz/NLBrute, RDP fan-out, and service-registry C2 blobs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE post-injection C2 pattern where shellcode is injected into legitimate SyncHost.exe or svchost.exe which then beacons out. SyncHost.exe reaching the public internet is inherently anomalous, and svchost.exe egress to the known C2 is a direct hit — both are the article's named injection targets in the espionage and Gunra chains. Rationale: The article and corroborating AhnLab report name svchost.exe and SyncHost.exe as the specific injection targets; SyncHost.exe public egress is behaviourally rare, and svchost.exe to the named C2 IP scopes the noisy svchost case to a hard indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1055.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SyncHost.exe legitimately syncing UWP/Mail-Calendar app data to Microsoft cloud endpoints (filter *.microsoft.com)
  • svchost.exe Windows Update / telemetry to Microsoft IP ranges (excluded via 20.* and MS domains)
  • Third-party sync client mis-named synchost.exe
  • Proxy/NAT collapsing many hosts behind one svchost egress record
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".live.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".office.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the remote IP is non-Microsoft; a SyncHost.exe connection to an unfamiliar VPS or the C2 IP is a true positive — pull the parent and any CreateRemoteThread (Sysmon 8) targeting the process. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture memory before the in-memory PE is wiped. 3) Hunt: check the same host for AnySign4PC exploitation, encrypted service-registry C2 blobs, and reverse-tunnel egress to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SyncHost.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26")
| where RemoteIP !startswith "20." and RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".windowsupdate.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "176.65.128.26") or (tolower(tostring(split(SrcHostname,"\\")[-1])) == "synchost.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SIGNBT/Gunra payload staging via net.tmp and inet.tmp AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or execution of the payload files net.tmp and inet.tmp — filenames AhnLab confirms were reused across both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains, with net.tmp invoked with a GUID-format argument. Detects both the file drop and the rundll32/loader execution referencing these temp payloads. Rationale: net.tmp and inet.tmp are exact malware filenames AhnLab confirms across both operations, with net.tmp carrying a GUID-format argument; matching them in command lines and file drops is high-fidelity and rarely benign. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.011 T1027.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate installer or app that happens to write a temp file literally named net.tmp/inet.tmp (rare; verify parent and path)
  • Network-config tooling logging to a *net.tmp scratch file
  • Backup/AV quarantine renaming a file to net.tmp coincidentally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","svchost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the file hash and the full command line — a GUID argument passed to net.tmp via rundll32/a loader is a strong true positive; the loader may side-load a DLL. 2) Contain: isolate the host and image memory (files may be deleted post-load and restored only at clean shutdown with a different hash). 3) Hunt: correlate with AnySign4PC exploitation, service-registry C2 blobs, and 176.65.128[.]26 egress; the same filenames appearing elsewhere may indicate the Gunra pre-ransomware stage.
let Drops = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="FileCreate", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let Exec = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="Exec", FileName, FolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
Drops | union Exec
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "net.tmp" or CommandLine has "inet.tmp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

COPPERHEDGE/SIGNBT C2 config in service-registry blobs + unusual service creation AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the article's named persistence/C2-storage pattern: backdoors that read command-and-control information from encrypted blobs stored under service-registry entries, paired with unusual service creation. Flags registry value writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services whose ImagePath points at ProgramData/Temp/AppData. Rationale: The article and AhnLab explicitly recommend hunting 'encrypted data stored under service-registry entries' and 'unusual service creation'; scoping registry writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services running from ProgramData/Temp targets that exact tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1112 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate driver/service installers writing binary config under Services keys via a non-standard installer
  • EDR/AV agents storing encrypted config blobs under their own service key
  • Backup or management agents installed from ProgramData with a service entry
  • GPO/SCCM software deployment creating services from staging paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "setup.exe" and RegistryKey !has "Sense" and RegistryKey !has "WinDefend"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and the service ImagePath — a rundll32/unsigned binary writing a REG_BINARY blob under a Services key, or a service pointing at Temp/ProgramData, is a true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, export the registry blob for offline decryption, and disable the rogue service. 3) Hunt: extract C2 from the decrypted blob and sweep for egress to those IPs plus 176.65.128[.]26, and check for svchost/SyncHost injection on the same host.
let SvcRegBlob = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueType == "Binary"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="SvcRegBlob", RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let SvcInstall = DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="SvcInstall", RegistryKey=FolderPath, RegistryValueName=FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
SvcRegBlob | union SvcInstall
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceFileName has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, SubjectUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentControlSet\Services\* OR *\currentcontrolset\services\*) -@Image:(*\services.exe OR *\svchost.exe OR *\msiexec.exe OR *\TrustedInstaller.exe)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate RegObjectName=/\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(services|svchost|msiexec|trustedinstaller)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*" AND Registry.registry_value_type="REG_BINARY" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| where NOT process_name IN ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","System")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*" AND Registry.registry_value_type="REG_BINARY" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| where NOT process_name IN ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","System")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Anti-forensic evidence destruction: SDelete / CCleaner + 4-char rename-then-delete AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's named anti-forensic routine: renaming malicious files to random four-character names before deletion, with additional wiping via SDelete and CCleaner observed by Plainbit. Detects SDelete/CCleaner execution and the rename-to-4-char-name-then-delete file sequence. Rationale: Plainbit specifically observed SDelete and CCleaner used for evidence destruction, and AhnLab documented the rename-to-random-4-char-name-before-delete routine; combining the named tools with the rename/delete file pattern targets this exact anti-forensic tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1485 T1070.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using SDelete legitimately to securely wipe free space or decommission a disk
  • IT running CCleaner as a sanctioned cleanup/maintenance tool
  • Software installers creating short temp filenames that get renamed/deleted normally
  • Backup software renaming files to short hashes during dedup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccleaner.exe","CCUpdate.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files") and AccountName !in~ ("itadmin","backupsvc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check who/what launched the wiper — SDelete/CCleaner run by a non-admin user, a service account, or a process descended from AnySign4PC/svchost is a true positive; correlate rename-to-4-char events on the same host and time window. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (evidence is being destroyed) and preserve any remaining volatile memory and MFT. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host's exploitation, injection, and C2 indicators before artifacts are gone, and check for lateral movement (RDP, NLBrute) to other hosts.
let Wipers = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "sdelete" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","-s","-nobanner"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="WiperExec", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName;
let RenameWipe = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileRenamed"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[A-Za-z0-9]{4}(\.[A-Za-z0-9]{1,4})?$"
| where PreviousFileName endswith ".dll" or PreviousFileName endswith ".tmp" or PreviousFileName endswith ".exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="RenameToRandom", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName=PreviousFileName;
Wipers | union RenameWipe
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (CommandLine has "sdelete" and CommandLine has_any ("-p","-nobanner"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("176.65.128.26")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append

        where Web.dest IN ("jshosting.me")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("jshosting.me")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-30 12 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unit 42 details a Chinese speaking threat actor combining autonomous AI scanning across seven vulnerabilities with manual exploitation. Read more. The post Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Autonomous mass-scan burst: langflow_poc.py multi-threaded FOFA target sweep · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow CVE-2026-33017 unauthenticated RCE exploitation (build_public_tmp) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hermes Agent autonomous attack framework execution (fofoapi.py / FofaMap MCP) · [LLM] AI coding-tool anti-attribution / permission-bypass config artifacts
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to AI-tool anonymizing proxy code.newcli[.]com (knaithe/KnYuan campaign) · [LLM] Direct egress to Chinese-market LLM APIs (DeepSeek/Qwen) from the estate · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Egress to AI-tool anonymizing proxy code.newcli[.]com (knaithe/KnYuan campaign) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections/DNS to code.newcli[.]com, the third-party proxy the actor used to front Claude Code (/ultra) and Codex (/codex/v1) traffic and reduce traceability. Any estate host resolving or connecting to this domain is either the actor's tooling host or a compromised relay. Rationale: code.newcli[.]com is a hard IOC named in Table 1 as the proxy fronting both Western AI tools; the /ultra and /codex/v1 sub-paths are actor-specific. Very low FP as this is not a mainstream service. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A curious developer manually evaluating the same third-party AI proxy service
  • Security researcher replicating the Unit 42 analysis in a lab
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling auto-resolving IOCs from a feed
  • Sandbox/detonation VM fetching the domain during malware analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process/user on the host that resolved code.newcli[.]com — legitimate AI-coding tools do not route through this proxy. 2) CONTAIN: Block newcli.com at the proxy/firewall and isolate the host if the process is an unsanctioned agent framework (python, node, hermes). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host for egress to api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com, and for langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py execution to confirm the autonomous-attack tooling.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "newcli.com" or RemoteUrl has_any ("code.newcli.com/ultra","code.newcli.com/codex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "newcli.com" or RequestURL has "code.newcli.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to AI-Tool Anonymizing Proxy code.newcli.com
id: 6f1c2e14-2a7d-4b9e-8c31-9a1f0b7d4e21
description: Detects egress to code.newcli[.]com, the proxy used by the knaithe/KnYuan autonomous AI attack campaign to front Claude Code and Codex API traffic.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1090.003
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains: 'newcli.com'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*newcli.com OR *NEWCLI.COM)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/newcli\.com$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*code.newcli.com*" OR Web.dest="code.newcli.com" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_user_agent, Web.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*code.newcli.com*" OR Web.dest="code.newcli.com" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.http_user_agent, Web.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Direct egress to Chinese-market LLM APIs (DeepSeek/Qwen) from the estate AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts direct API calls to api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com, the native endpoints the actor hit directly (bypassing the proxy) for DeepSeek and Qwen/GLM/Kimi/MiniMax reasoning. Non-developer estate hosts reaching these are candidate autonomous-attack operator nodes. Rationale: api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com are the exact native API endpoints in Table 1 the actor used directly. FP medium because legitimate developers may evaluate these models — pivot on non-dev hosts and pair with tooling process names. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers or data-science teams legitimately trialing DeepSeek/Qwen APIs
  • AI gateway/enterprise proxy that aggregates multiple model providers
  • Marketing/research staff using consumer AI chat clients
  • CI pipeline calling a model API for code assistance
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the host belongs to a sanctioned developer/data-science group and whether the initiating process is a browser vs a scripting/agent runtime (python/node). 2) CONTAIN: If the host is a server or non-dev endpoint running an agent framework, isolate and revoke any local API keys found. 3) HUNT: Correlate with code.newcli[.]com egress, langflow_poc.py/fofoapi.py execution and outbound FOFA queries to confirm autonomous-operator activity vs benign model use.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Procs=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName in~ ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com") or RequestURL has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Langflow CVE-2026-33017 unauthenticated RCE exploitation (build_public_tmp) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound exploitation of Langflow's unauthenticated code-execution surface (CVE-2026-33017, CVSS 9.8) against internet-facing Langflow instances the campaign enumerated via FOFA title="Langflow". Targets POST traffic to the Langflow code-validation API and mass-scan patterns from the actor's langflow_poc.py. Rationale: Grounded in the article's Langflow phase: FOFA title="Langflow", langflow_poc.py scanner and CVE-2026-33017 (CVSS 9.8). Endpoint /api/v1/validate/code is Langflow's documented unauthenticated code-execution surface; note in rationale it is derived from Langflow CVE knowledge, not verbatim from the article which did not print the path. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://github.com/oscar-mine/CVE-2026-33017-Exploit
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users saving/validating custom Python components via the UI
  • Internal QA/regression tests exercising the Langflow API
  • Authenticated automation pipelines building flows programmatically
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) safe-checking the endpoint
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Langflow instance version (1.3.4 was vulnerable per the article) and whether auto_login or a public flow ID is enabled — the exploit only succeeds with those prerequisites. 2) CONTAIN: Put Langflow behind authentication, disable auto_login, and block the scanning source IPs at the WAF. 3) HUNT: Review web logs for the same source IP fingerprint hitting many hosts rapidly (mass FOFA-enumerated scan), and check the Langflow host for post-exploit child processes spawned by the app runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| summarize Hits=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent,10) by Computer, cIP, csUriStem
| where Hits >= 1
| order by Hits desc

Hermes Agent autonomous attack framework execution (fofoapi.py / FofaMap MCP) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of the actor's autonomous offensive tooling on estate hosts: the Hermes Agent framework and its custom fofoapi.py FOFA-enumeration script / FofaMap-Platinum MCP server driving DeepSeek. Catches the operator node itself rather than the victim. Rationale: fofoapi.py, fofa-cyberspace-search, FofaMap-Platinum-Full-Expert MCP, web-terminal-exploitation and godmode are custom, campaign-unique skill/script names from the Technical Analysis section — extremely low chance of benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red team or purple team replaying the Hermes Agent tooling in a sanctioned exercise
  • Security researcher analyzing the recovered toolset in a lab
  • Threat-intel analyst naming files after the IOCs during investigation
  • A benign unrelated project coincidentally naming a script 'fofoapi.py' (rare)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is not a sanctioned red-team box; capture the full command line, parent process and user. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, snapshot memory/disk, and pull any Hermes Agent config/session logs and Telegram C2 tokens for IR. 3) HUNT: Enumerate the host's home directory for an exposed file server (the article's OPSEC failure), and pivot on outbound FOFA queries, DeepSeek/Qwen API egress and code.newcli[.]com traffic.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("fofoapi.py","fofa-cyberspace-search","FofaMap-Platinum","web-terminal-exploitation","godmode")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)hermes[-_ ]?agent"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("fofoapi.py","fofa-cyberspace-search","FofaMap-Platinum","web-terminal-exploitation") or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)hermes[-_ ]?agent"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding-tool anti-attribution / permission-bypass config artifacts AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the actor's tell-tale AI-tool hardening: disabling attribution headers and response storage and forcing auto-approval so the agents run unattended. Detects the specific config keys and CLI flags (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0, disable_response_storage=true, dangerously-skip-permissions, approvalMode yolo) on estate hosts. Rationale: These are verbatim config keys/flags from Table 1 and the Tool Configuration section (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER:0, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC:1, disable_response_storage=true, dangerously-skip-permissions:true, approvalMode:yolo). Medium FP because a careless developer could set some of these; the combination or presence on a non-dev host is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1070
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions for a trusted local task
  • CI automation setting approvalMode to a non-interactive value
  • Privacy-conscious user disabling telemetry/response storage
  • AI-tool documentation or tutorial commands copy-pasted into a shell
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ () or isnotempty(DeviceName)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine which AI tool set the flag, the user, and whether the host is a sanctioned developer machine. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, isolate the host and preserve the tool config directories (.claude, codex config, qwen config) plus any 'trusted directory' allowlists. 3) HUNT: Correlate with code.newcli[.]com and DeepSeek/Qwen egress and with Hermes Agent / fofoapi.py execution to distinguish a careless dev from the autonomous-attack operator.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dangerously-skip-permissions","CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","disable_response_storage")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)approvalMode\s*[:=]\s*.?yolo"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dangerously-skip-permissions","CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","disable_response_storage") or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)approvalMode\s*[:=]\s*.?yolo"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Autonomous mass-scan burst: langflow_poc.py multi-threaded FOFA target sweep AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the discovery/scanning phase where the Hermes Agent ran langflow_poc.py against a FOFA-enumerated target file at high concurrency (--scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10). Detects the scanner process and the resulting rapid outbound connection burst characteristic of automated, not human-paced, probing. Rationale: langflow_poc.py, langflow_targets.txt and the --scan-file/--threads 10 flags are the exact command from the Langflow phase; combining the process identity with a public-target fan-out burst (>=10 distinct targets/5m matching the --threads 10 concurrency) separates automated scanning from human pacing. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://github.com/oscar-mine/CVE-2026-33017-Exploit
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned internal vulnerability scanning of Langflow assets by the AppSec team
  • A pentester running the public PoC during an authorized engagement
  • Asset-inventory tooling probing internal Langflow ports (7860)
  • Load testing of a Langflow deployment generating many concurrent connections
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the scanning host is not sanctioned scanning infrastructure and review the command line and target file contents (langflow_targets.txt). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block its outbound scanning, and preserve the target list and PoC binary for scope assessment. 3) HUNT: Enrich the target IPs to find which are your own internet-facing Langflow instances, then check those instances for successful POST /api/v1/validate/code exploitation and post-exploit child processes.
let ScannerHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "langflow_poc.py" or ProcessCommandLine has "langflow_targets.txt" or (ProcessCommandLine has "--scan-file" and ProcessCommandLine has "--threads")
| distinct DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceId in (ScannerHosts)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and RemotePort in (7860, 80, 443)
| summarize DistinctTargets=dcount(RemoteIP), Conns=count(), Window=max(Timestamp)-min(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 10   // 10 = actor's --threads 10 concurrency against many FOFA targets in a tight window
| order by DistinctTargets desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "langflow_poc.py" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "langflow_targets.txt" or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--scan-file" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--threads")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

Toy Ghouls’ new toy: the GenieLocker ransomware

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-30 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Kaspersky experts dissect GenieLocker: new custom ransomware variants for Windows, Linux, and ESXi systems. We found this family in attacks by Toy Ghouls, a financially motivated extortion group.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1021.002 T1190 T1204.002 T1486
IPs89.125.66.101
MD5a50eaaf514f4f84e… f08f476f26b01d14… fd46a80c2f455772… de3cfbb50f66079b… 780c8f4c6f077da4…
