Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe) execution for internal discovery
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] External-partner VPN logon with valid credentials (trusted-relationship abuse)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Toy Ghouls’ new toy: the GenieLocker ransomware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] socks5.exe / anomalous Windows OpenSSH server for pivot tunneling · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Reverse SSH tunnel and C2 beacon to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GenieLocker Windows ransomware execution via secret-argument hex + --percent/--recursive flags · [LLM] Mimikatz credential dumping via command-line/module signature · [LLM] KeePassXC .kdbx vault access/copy by non-KeePass process · [LLM] GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi via --percent/--recursive flags · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change
GenieLocker Windows ransomware execution via secret-argument hex + --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts execution of the GenieLocker PE encryptor, which requires a long hex 'secret argument' as its first parameter and exposes distinctive --percent/-p and --recursive/-r CLI flags plus a -l/--log path. Anchors on the confirmed Windows sample MD5 and the malware's unique command-line shape. Rationale: Uses the article's confirmed Windows sample MD5 (5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c) and the malware's documented argument table (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log) — the --percent+--recursive combination is a rare, high-fidelity anchor for an encryptor. Cross-checked with gbhackers and mallory.ai malware profiles. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/ • https://mallory.ai/malware/019d2af9-67da-7113-b5e6-2e6c809b97b1
ATT&CKT1486 T1480.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A backup/imaging utility invoked with both --percent (progress) and --recursive flags
  • Custom sysadmin file-processing scripts that mirror those long-flag names
  • Security-team detonation of the sample in a sandbox using the real secret argument
  • File-integrity or compression tools with a --recursive + --log combination
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.manager.exe","veeamagent.exe") and MD5 != "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent process; confirm the first argument is a long hex string and MD5 matches a GenieLocker sample. Check the target path passed as the last argument. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network immediately, kill the process tree, and preserve volatile memory before shutdown to avoid losing per-file keys. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same MD5 and the --percent/--recursive command line across all hosts (mass deployment via PsExec/PAExec is expected), and look for preceding netscan.exe/mimikatz/socks5.exe activity on the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where MD5 == "5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, MD5, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "--percent" and CommandLine has "--recursive") or (CommandLine has "--percent" and CommandLine has "--log")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GenieLocker Windows Ransomware Execution (secret-arg + encrypt flags)
id: 7c3a1e42-9f1b-4c67-b0e2-1a4d9b2c8e10
description: Detects GenieLocker PE encryptor via its confirmed MD5 or its distinctive --percent/--recursive/--log command-line flags.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1486
  - attack.t1480.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_hash:
    MD5: '5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c'
  selection_cli:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--percent'
      - '--recursive'
  condition: selection_hash or selection_cli
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate archivers or backup CLIs that coincidentally use --percent and --recursive together
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Hashes:*5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c* OR (@CommandLine:*--percent* AND @CommandLine:*--recursive*) OR (@CommandLine:*--percent* AND @CommandLine:*--log*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| MD5HashData=/^5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c$/i OR (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--recursive", field=CommandLine)) OR (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--log", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, MD5HashData], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_hash="5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c" OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_hash="5d62c1349b8981c396c9a23f4f8f053c" OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where user!="*$" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
External-partner VPN logon with valid credentials (trusted-relationship abuse) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the GenieLocker initial-access vector: successful network/RDP logons using valid domain credentials that originate from a public (external partner) IP, consistent with the reported OpenVPN entry from a trusted partner's network. Flags externally-sourced authenticated sessions that precede internal tooling activity. Rationale: Grounded in the article's explicit initial-access statement (OpenVPN from an external partner network with stolen-but-valid credentials, T1199 trusted relationship). Detects authenticated sessions sourced from public IPs — the observable signature of externally-terminated VPN/RDP access with valid accounts. Confirmed by cybersecuritynews and gbhackers write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1078 T1199
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate partner/vendor remote support sessions over VPN or RDP
  • Remote employees connecting from home ISPs when the VPN gateway forwards the real public source IP
  • Cloud-hosted jump boxes with public NICs authenticating to domain resources
  • Split-tunnel VPN configurations that expose the client's public IP on network logons
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("<approved-partner-vpn-egress-not-applicable>") == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate the RemoteIP and confirm whether it belongs to a sanctioned partner range; verify the account is expected to authenticate externally and whether MFA was satisfied. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, disable the account, force credential reset, and terminate active sessions at the VPN concentrator. 3) Hunt: pivot on the account across DeviceProcessEvents for netscan.exe/mimikatz/socks5.exe and on DeviceLogonEvents for subsequent RDP/SSH lateral movement to other hosts.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "LogonSuccess"
| where LogonType in ("Network","RemoteInteractive")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hosts=make_set(DeviceName,20), Count=count() by AccountName, RemoteIP, LogonType
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4624
| where LogonType in (3,10)
| where isnotempty(IpAddress) and IpAddress !in ("-","::1","127.0.0.1")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(IpAddress))
| where TargetUserName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Hosts=make_set(Computer,20) by TargetUserName, IpAddress, LogonType
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4624 @LogonType:(3 OR 10) NOT (CIDR(@IpAddress, 10.0.0.0/8) OR CIDR(@IpAddress, 172.16.0.0/12) OR CIDR(@IpAddress, 192.168.0.0/16)) -@TargetUserName:*$

SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe) execution for internal discovery AIReconnaissance High
Detects the SoftPerfect Network Scanner used by Toy Ghouls for host/network discovery, matching on the netscan.exe image name and, resiliently, on the SoftPerfect vendor/product version metadata so renamed copies are still caught. Rationale: Article names 'SoftPerfect Network Scanner' as the discovery tool. Anchoring on both the netscan.exe image name and the SoftPerfect product/company PE metadata defeats simple renames while staying specific to this campaign's toolset. Corroborated by gbhackers and cybersecuritynews. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned IT teams using SoftPerfect Network Scanner for asset inventory
  • Network engineers troubleshooting connectivity with the same tool
  • MSP/consultant onboarding scans
  • Vulnerability-management pilots evaluating SoftPerfect
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-itasset","svc-netmon")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing account and host are authorized to run network-scanning tools; review the scan's target ranges in the command line/config. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, isolate the host and disable the account pending review. 3) Hunt: on the same host/account look for Mimikatz command lines, socks5.exe/sshd.exe, and outbound connections to 89.125.66.101 — netscan is typically the discovery step that precedes credential access and lateral movement.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "netscan.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "netscan.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "Network Scanner"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "SoftPerfect"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\netscan.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mimikatz credential dumping via command-line/module signature AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Mimikatz execution used by Toy Ghouls to dump credentials, anchoring on its signature command modules (sekurlsa::, lsadump::, privilege::debug) and PE metadata rather than LSASS memory access, so renamed binaries are still caught. Rationale: Article states Mimikatz was used to dump credentials. Matching on module strings (sekurlsa::/lsadump::/privilege::debug) and gentilkiwi PE metadata is high-fidelity and deliberately avoids the pre-existing generic LSASS-access rule. Corroborated by cybersecuritynews and gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/genielocker-ransomware-attack/
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned red-team/pentest engagements running Mimikatz
  • Security tooling that bundles Mimikatz modules for detection testing
  • EDR/AV signature files containing the module strings scanned into a command line (rare)
  • Purple-team detection-validation exercises
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "redteam" and DeviceName !in~ ("PURPLELAB01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent process; confirm elevation (privilege::debug requires admin) and whether an active red-team engagement is scheduled. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset credentials for every account that had a session on it, and rotate service-account/krbtgt if domain admin material was exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot on the harvested accounts across DeviceLogonEvents for RDP/SSH lateral movement and on KeePassXC .kdbx access on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","lsadump::","privilege::debug","kerberos::","crypto::","mimikatz")
   or FileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName =~ "mimikatz.exe"
   or ProcessVersionInfoFileDescription has "mimikatz"
   or ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "gentilkiwi"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("sekurlsa::","lsadump::","privilege::debug","kerberos::","mimikatz")
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\mimikatz.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

KeePassXC .kdbx vault access/copy by non-KeePass process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects attempts to steal credentials from KeePassXC databases, as reported in the intrusion: a .kdbx file being created/copied or referenced in a command line by any process other than KeePassXC/KeePass (shells, archivers, copy utilities). Rationale: Article states the actors accessed KeePassXC databases on several hosts to extract stored credentials. A .kdbx write/copy by anything other than the KeePass client is a targeted, high-signal credential-store theft indicator (T1555.005). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
ATT&CKT1555.005 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup agents (Veeam, CrashPlan, OneDrive/Backup) copying profile folders containing .kdbx
  • A user manually copying their own vault to a USB drive or network share
  • File-sync clients (Dropbox/Nextcloud) replicating a .kdbx
  • Migration tooling moving a user profile to a new machine
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeamagent.exe","onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","backup.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\Backup\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and destination path — a copy to Temp/Public/network share or an archiver (7z/rar) reading .kdbx is high concern; a backup agent to a backup path is likely benign. 2) Contain: if malicious, isolate the host and force reset of every credential potentially stored in that vault. 3) Hunt: correlate with Mimikatz execution and outbound transfer/staging on the same host, and check whether the .kdbx was subsequently archived or moved toward the C2 IP 89.125.66.101.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("keepassxc.exe","keepass.exe","keepassxc-cli.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".kdbx"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !has "keepass"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

socks5.exe / anomalous Windows OpenSSH server for pivot tunneling AIInstallation Medium
Detects the pivot/tunneling toolkit Toy Ghouls installed on compromised Windows hosts — the named socks5.exe proxy binary, an OpenSSH sshd.exe server running on a Windows endpoint, and ssh.exe dynamic-SOCKS (-D) proxying — used to build lateral-movement infrastructure. Rationale: Article lists socks5.exe and OpenSSH among tools installed on compromised hosts for pivoting. socks5.exe is a specific binary name; an sshd.exe server or ssh -D dynamic proxy on Windows endpoints is anomalous tunneling infrastructure (T1572/T1090). Confirmed by gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://gbhackers.com/new-genielocker-ransomware-encrypts-windows-linux-and-vmware-esxi-systems/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1021.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Servers where Windows OpenSSH Server (sshd.exe) is a sanctioned, installed role
  • Developers/admins using ssh -D for legitimate SOCKS forwarding
  • Third-party VPN or remote-access software that bundles a socks proxy component
  • Automation/CI agents launching sshd for build tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "sshd.exe" and DeviceName in~ ("LINUXJUMP01","SSHGW01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether OpenSSH Server / SOCKS proxying is an approved service on this host; review the binary path (Temp/Public/user profile = suspicious) and command-line listen ports. 2) Contain: kill the process, block the listening port, and isolate the host if the tooling is unsanctioned. 3) Hunt: check DeviceNetworkEvents from this host to 89.125.66.101 and for inbound connections to the socks/ssh listener from other internal hosts (pivot fan-out).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "socks5.exe"
   or FileName =~ "sshd.exe"
   or (FileName =~ "ssh.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-D")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\socks5.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\\sshd.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\\ssh.exe" and CommandLine has "-D")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: socks5.exe / Anomalous OpenSSH Server on Windows (Toy Ghouls pivot)

Reverse SSH tunnel and C2 beacon to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the reverse SSH tunnel Toy Ghouls established for command-and-control: any outbound connection to the confirmed C2 IP 89.125.66.101, and ssh.exe/plink reverse-forwarding (-R) to a public host — the network signature of the C2 channel. Rationale: IP 89.125.66.101 is the article's C2 indicator (corroborated by the Securelist IOC list and mallory.ai). Combined with ssh.exe/plink '-R' reverse-forwarding to public destinations — the exact reverse-SSH-tunnel C2 technique the article describes — this is a high-fidelity C2 detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://mallory.ai/malware/019d2af9-67da-7113-b5e6-2e6c809b97b1
ATT&CKT1572 T1071 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/allowlist scanners or sinkholes deliberately touching the IOC
  • Security researchers detonating samples in a monitored lab
  • Admins using ssh -R for legitimate reverse-forwarding to a sanctioned bastion
  • Netflow re-ingestion causing historical hits after the IOC is already remediated
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threatintel" and DeviceName !in~ ("MALWARELAB01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (ContextImageFileName/InitiatingProcessFileName) and account driving the connection to 89.125.66.101; determine direction and byte volume. 2) Contain: block 89.125.66.101 at the perimeter, isolate the beaconing host, and terminate any ssh.exe/plink -R sessions. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for connections to the IP and for socks5.exe/sshd.exe pivot infrastructure, then check for GenieLocker execution (UC1) as encryption often follows C2 setup.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "89.125.66.101"
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ssh.exe","plink.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "-R" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "89.125.66.101"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to GenieLocker C2 89.125.66.101

GenieLocker ELF encryptor on Linux/ESXi via --percent/--recursive flags AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GenieLocker ELF build used to encrypt Linux servers and ESXi datastores after stopping running VMs. Anchors on the shared encryptor CLI flags (--percent/-p, --recursive/-r, --log/-l) executed on Linux hosts. Rationale: Article documents an ELF GenieLocker build encrypting Linux/ESXi servers after stopping VMs, sharing the same argument set (-p/--percent, -r/--recursive, -l/--log) as the Windows build. Scoping those flags to Linux process telemetry targets the ESXi/Linux impact phase. Cross-platform behaviour confirmed by technadu and gbhackers. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/ • https://www.technadu.com/genielocker-ransomware-targets-windows-linux-and-esxi-systems-leaves-no-ransom-note/632252/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Linux backup or rsync-style utilities invoked with --percent progress and --recursive together
  • ESXi/admin maintenance scripts that batch-process datastore files with similar flags
  • Media/transcoding jobs using --recursive over a tree with a --log destination
  • Legitimate encryption/compression CLI tools run by admins
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("rsync","tar","borg","restic","duplicity")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the path argument; on ESXi correlate with recent vmsvc power-off / VM shutdown activity and check the binary against GenieLocker ELF hashes. 2) Contain: kill the process, disconnect the host/datastore from the network, and protect backups/snapshots from deletion. 3) Hunt: check SSH access logs for the reverse tunnel and connections to 89.125.66.101, and review other Linux/ESXi hosts reachable over SSH for the same flag pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| where FolderPath startswith "/" or FolderPath has "/tmp/" or FolderPath has "/var/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux" or ActingProcessName startswith "/"
| where (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--recursive")
     or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--percent" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--log")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GenieLocker ELF Encryptor Execution on Linux/ESXi
id: 8b1e4d02-5c39-47a6-9e70-3d2f6a1c9b84
description: Detects the GenieLocker ELF build on Linux/ESXi via its --percent/--recursive/--log encryptor flags.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/04
tags:
  - attack.t1486
  - attack.t1490
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_pr:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--percent'
      - '--recursive'
  selection_log:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '--percent'
      - '--log'
  condition: selection_pr or selection_log
falsepositives:
  - Linux CLI backup/compression utilities that accept --percent and --recursive together
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:(*--percent* AND *--recursive*) OR @process.command_line:(*--percent* AND *--log*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 event_platform=Lin
| (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--recursive", field=CommandLine)) OR (regex("--percent", field=CommandLine) AND regex("--log", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) AND Processes.os="Linux" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--recursive*") OR (Processes.process="*--percent*" AND Processes.process="*--log*")) AND Processes.os="Linux" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a50eaaf514f4f84e61ca2455a8789753", "f08f476f26b01d142ca73923de65fc0c", "fd46a80c2f45577263328984edf7f4dc", "de3cfbb50f66079bfee20a6f64e59433",         | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)

        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate

            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: critical

// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("socks5.exe", "config.msi", "kftd.exe", "genie_encrypt.exe", "run.exe", "run2.exe", "genie.exe", "consultant.exe", "tempo.exe", "kernel.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

// File-creation events for the named binaries / paths
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/vmware/welcome") or FileName in~ ("socks5.exe", "config.msi", "kftd.exe", "genie_encrypt.exe", "run.exe", "run2.exe", "genie.exe", "consultant.exe", "tempo.exe", "kernel.exe"))

          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Recon tool reading K8s service-account token or /proc/self/environ inside a container AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts an interactive/recon binary (cat, curl, python, base64, xxd) reading the mounted Kubernetes service-account token path or /proc/self/environ inside a workload — the day-1 in-pod enumeration the article describes ('a pod reading /proc/self/environ, inspecting service-account tokens'). Distinguishes credential/environment harvesting from a normal application startup read. Rationale: Uses the article's literal strings '/proc/self/environ' and 'service-account tokens' (mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount) plus recon-tool binaries, so it fires on enumeration rather than a library's normal token read. Cross-checked the K8s SA-token-theft chain in Unit42 and TheHackerNews' breach coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/openai-agent-used-exposed-credentials.html • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/modern-kubernetes-threats/ • https://aquilax.ai/blog/kubernetes-service-account-token-theft
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1613 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Init container or entrypoint script that cats the SA token for debugging
  • CI/CD job (e.g. Helm, kubectl-in-pod) echoing token path during setup
  • Observability agent reading /proc/<pid>/environ for process metadata enrichment
  • Developer running an interactive shell in a pod during troubleshooting
  • Security scanner/CIS-benchmark tool auditing token mounts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("kubelet","containerd","dockerd") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("entrypoint","docker-entrypoint","helm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the pod/node (DeviceName), the process lineage, and whether the reader is the workload's own app or an injected shell/tool; pull the full command line and parent. 2) Contain: if the reader is not the expected app, cordon the node, kill the pod, and rotate the pod's service-account token and any secrets it could reach. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for subsequent connections to 169.254.169.254 (IMDS), privileged pod creation in K8s audit, and outbound to pastebin/request-capture/file-sharing services indicating C2 staging.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("cat","head","tail","curl","wget","python","python3","sh","bash","dash","busybox","base64","xxd","strings")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount","/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount","/proc/self/environ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cat","head","tail","curl","wget","python","python3","sh","bash","busybox","base64","xxd","strings")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount","/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount","/proc/self/environ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Recon Tool Reading K8s Service-Account Token or Process Environ in Container
id: 8b1d2f34-6a7c-4e19-9b2a-1c4e7f0a9d21
description: Detects an interactive or recon binary reading the mounted Kubernetes service-account token path or /proc/self/environ inside a container, consistent with the Hugging Face agent breach day-1 in-pod enumeration.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/hugging-face-open-ai-breach-takeaways
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/modern-kubernetes-threats/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/30
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1613
  - attack.t1528
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/cat'
      - '/head'
      - '/tail'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/busybox'
      - '/base64'
      - '/xxd'
      - '/strings'
  selection_path:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount'
      - '/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount'
      - '/proc/self/environ'
  condition: selection_img and selection_path
falsepositives:
  - Init containers or CI jobs that legitimately cat the service-account token for debugging
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*serviceaccount/token* OR @process.command_line:*proc/self/environ* OR @process.command_line:*secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount*) @process.name:(cat OR head OR curl OR wget OR python OR python3 OR sh OR bash OR busybox OR base64 OR xxd OR strings)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(cat|head|tail|curl|wget|python[0-9]?|sh|bash|busybox|base64|xxd|strings)$/i
| regex("(/var/run/secrets/kubernetes\\.io/serviceaccount|/run/secrets/kubernetes\\.io/serviceaccount|/proc/self/environ)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("cat","head","tail","curl","wget","python","python3","sh","bash","busybox","base64","xxd","strings")) (Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount*" OR Processes.process="*/proc/self/environ*" OR Processes.process="*/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("cat","head","tail","curl","wget","python","python3","sh","bash","busybox","base64","xxd","strings")) (Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount*" OR Processes.process="*/proc/self/environ*" OR Processes.process="*/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Cloud instance metadata (IMDS 169.254.169.254) queried by a recon tool inside a workload AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a container-side recon binary (curl, wget, python, busybox) connecting to the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254 / 169.254.170.2) — the article's 'queried cloud metadata' step used to harvest node IAM credentials. Filtering on the recon tool separates credential theft from legitimate cloud-SDK IMDS calls. Rationale: Anchors on the well-known IMDS IPs (169.254.169.254 for AWS/Azure/GCP, 169.254.170.2 for ECS) paired with recon binaries, matching the article's 'queried cloud metadata' credential-harvest step while excluding in-app SDK IMDS traffic. IMDS-to-IAM abuse corroborated by Unit42/SecureByDezign. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/modern-kubernetes-threats/ • https://www.securebydezign.com/articles/kubernetes-pod-escape-cloud-takeover.html
ATT&CKT1552.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • cloud-init / bootstrap scripts curling IMDS for instance identity or user-data
  • kube2iam / kiam / IRDS sidecars that proxy IMDS via curl-like helpers
  • Health-check scripts querying instance-id or region from metadata
  • aws-cli/gcloud shell wrappers invoked by legitimate automation
  • Debugging session where an engineer manually curls IMDS
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cloud-init","user-data","kube2iam","instance-id","api-token"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the initiating process command line — did it hit the credentials path (/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ or /computeMetadata/v1/) and was IMDSv2 token flow used? Identify the host/pod and its IAM role. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate the node or pod IAM role credentials, and add a GuardDuty/SCP guardrail; if creds were retrieved, assume they are compromised and rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot to CloudTrail for AssumeRole/API calls made with those temporary credentials from a source IP outside the VPC (see UC4), and check for privileged pod creation on the same node.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","python","python3","sh","bash","busybox","perl","ruby","nc","ncat")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254","169.254.170.2")
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound" or isempty(NetworkDirection)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
